name: Nutrigenomics diet

card.summary: A personalised-eating approach, often sold as a DNA diet, that uses genetic information to tailor food choices toward leaner body composition, clearer skin and better health.
card.aka: DNA diet, nutrigenetic diet, personalised nutrition
card.note: Direct-to-consumer genetic diet advice is a developing area; researchers describe the science of gene-diet interaction as still maturing.

quick.overview:
Nutrigenomics studies how nutrients affect gene expression, and its sister field nutrigenetics studies how a person's gene variants change their response to food. A nutrigenomics or DNA diet applies this idea by choosing foods or macronutrient ratios based on a person's genetic profile.

The appearance payoff is the one any diet offers: body fat, muscle and skin condition respond to what and how much a person eats, and personalised plans aim to make that eating more effective. Published reviews describe both promising gene-diet associations and the difficulty of turning them into advice.
quick.how: People typically order a consumer DNA or genetic-nutrition test, or work with a dietitian who interprets variants in genes tied to fat, carbohydrate or vitamin handling, then adjust their eating pattern, such as fat intake or Mediterranean-style choices, and track weight, bloodwork or skin. Results are monitored over weeks to months.
quick.risks: The diet itself is food-based, so direct physical risk is low. Reviews note that gene-diet associations are often modest and population-dependent, and genetic data raises privacy questions. Restrictive plans built from test results can leave out nutrients, so clinicians generally advise involving a dietitian.

lead: Nutrigenomics is the science of how dietary components influence gene expression, while nutrigenetics examines how genetic variation changes a person's response to nutrients; together they are called nutritional genomics.[1][4][8] A nutrigenomics or DNA diet puts this into practice by tailoring food recommendations to a person's genome, with the goal of improving body composition and health.

The appearance link is through body composition, skin and energy: genetic variants in genes such as FTO have been associated with different BMI outcomes depending on fat or carbohydrate intake,[8] and vitamin D is described as a leading nutrigenomic example because its active form acts on a nuclear receptor that regulates gene expression.[6] Marketing of personalised diets draws on this research.

Reviews describe the field as promising but still developing. A 2017 review of precision nutrition discusses personalised approaches for metabolic syndrome and the challenges of translating science into advice,[7] and a 2018 review covers precision nutrition for type 2 diabetes.[9]

chain: Genetic test or profile identifies diet-relevant variants
Food choices are adjusted to the profile
Eating pattern better matched to the person
Leaner physique and healthier skin over time
angle.text: Followers adjust fat, carbohydrate and nutrient intake according to genetic results, aiming for a more efficient diet. The appearance outcomes are those of the resulting diet: weight, muscle and skin.

infobox: Described as a new research field around 2001[5]

paras: Wikipedia treats nutrigenetics, nutrigenomics and nutritional epigenetics as subfields of nutritional genomics, studying how genes respond to nutrients and influence disease risk and traits.[5] A 2010 Annual Review of Public Health article argues that genome-wide association studies lack nutrient information needed for dietary advice, which nutrigenetics studies aim to supply.[2]

Examples cited include the FTO gene (the AA genotype linked to higher BMI under high-fat or low-carbohydrate intake), an APOB variant associated with obesity measures mainly in people eating a high-fat diet, apolipoprotein variants and responses to dietary lipids, and phenylketonuria, where nutrition can reverse symptoms.[5] A one-year lifestyle intervention found variants in APOA5 and ADIPOQ moderated metabolic syndrome improvements.[10] Reviews also discuss Mediterranean-diet effects on gene expression.[3][11]

A 2022 review describes each person as having a nutritional blueprint in their genes and anticipates personalised recommendations to maintain health and prevent disease.[1] A 2024 review frames genetics, nutrition and health as a new frontier in disease prevention.[12] Wikipedia notes that population variation can produce many more polymorphisms than a single SNP association captures, complicating simple gene-diet explanations.[5]

Randomized and interventional studies have examined diet effects on gene expression and genotype interactions: a 24-person randomized trial tested an apple and bergamot juice for oxidative stress and inflammation gene expression,[13] and a one-year lifestyle intervention examined genotype moderation of metabolic outcomes.[10] Trials of complete DNA-guided diet plans for appearance outcomes are not among these.

timeline.event: Nutritional genomics described as an emerging research field.[5]
